territorial_scope.description: Applies to City of Seattle departments and to vendors, contractors and volunteers operating on behalf of the City.

evidence.quote: All City departments. Vendors, contractors, and volunteers who operate on behalf of the City are also subject to this policy.

agora_harms: Violation of civil or human rights, including privacy

summary.short: Seattle policy POL-209, effective 11/1/2023, sets requirements for City departments, employees, and vendors or contractors acting for the City when acquiring and using generative AI. It requires pre-approval of tools, human review of outputs, attribution, equity review, data-privacy limits and records retention.
summary.long: Seattle policy POL-209 applies to all City departments, and to vendors, contractors and volunteers operating on behalf of the City. It covers software meeting its definition of generative artificial intelligence. It sets general AI principles (innovation, transparency, reliability, bias reduction, privacy, explainability, security) and states policy requirements for generative AI only. Acquisition of generative AI tools follows the City's technology acquisition standard, with pre-approved tools or exception requests reviewed by Seattle IT, which may approve, deny or revoke authorization. Outputs must be reviewed by humans before each official use, with documented review processes. Images, videos, substantive text and significant source code generated by AI must be attributed to the AI system, with a human review assertion. Departments must conduct a Racial Equity Toolkit before using generative AI tools. Confidential data may not be submitted unless enterprise controls are in place, and City data may not be used to train externally controlled models; tools that cannot prevent this may not be used. Prompts, outputs and inputs are treated as potentially public records, and vendors must support their retrieval and export. Exceptions require advance approval. The Chief Technology Officer is responsible for compliance, and non-compliance may lead to discipline, access restriction, or termination of employment or vendor contracts. The policy is effective 11/1/2023 and is to be reviewed annually.

relations.note: Section 5.1 requires generative AI use to be consistent with the City's Data Privacy Policy; matched to POL-202 by title, and the document does not give the match.
Section 5.1 requires generative AI use to be consistent with the City's Information Security Policy; matched to POL-201 by title.
Section 1.1 ties acquisition of generative AI tools to the City's standards for Acquisition of Technology Resources; section 1.3 applies that standard to free software and SaaS tools.
Section 5.2 bars submitting data classified as Confidential under the City's data classification guidelines to generative AI systems unless enterprise controls are in place.

notes: The text states no enabling act, amended or repealed instrument, or implemented instrument; the policy is an internal City policy, and the registry type 'guidance' is the registry's label. Section 5.1 names 'Data Privacy Policy' and 'Information Security Policy' without numbers; POL-202 and POL-201 are matched by title. Scope says vendors, contractors and volunteers are subject to the policy, but most operative duties are addressed to City employees and departments. Non-compliance consequences are employment, access or contract measures; no external penalty is stated. section_status is set to not_found because the schema requires it; the cross-references above are the relations found.

thresholds.note: The policy sets no numeric cutoffs that change legal treatment. Qualitative triggers exist but are not numbers: 'substantive use' in s.3.5 (departments interpret it) and 'significant amount of source code' in s.3.3. These are recorded as obligation triggers, not thresholds. The '4.0' in the s.3.4 example is a product version, not a threshold.
